<p align="center"><sub>80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).</sub></p>

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in.

CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code do the work. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license.

## Two ways to work

| | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off |
| How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-SOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox |
| You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running SOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node |
| Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs |

Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

<p align="center">
  <picture>
    <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/assets/readme/chat-home-dark.svg">
    <img src="docs/assets/readme/chat-home.svg" alt="The LoopForge chat workbench: a request is typed into the composer and the @ picker offers roles, skills, requirements and SOPs" width="100%">
  </picture>
</p>

<p align="center"><sub>The chat home. Type a request, <code>@</code> a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.</sub></p>

## Why LoopForge

Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships.

- **Repeatable.** Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs.
- **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat.
- **Human in the loop.** Approval gates where they matter. Read the report, approve, or send the work back to a chosen step.
- **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node.
- **Your stack, your servers.** CodeBuddy, Codex or Claude Code as executors. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime.

## Quick start

Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git
cd LoopForge
./start.sh
```

`./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source.

If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, set `MIRROR` to a registry host that can stand in for `ghcr.io`. `./start.sh` pulls from that host and tags the image back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`. Setting `MIRROR` trusts that host, because the download is tagged with the official name. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:<pin>` should show the same digest after `@`. Without `MIRROR`, `./start.sh` still pulls `ghcr.io` directly, and `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. Upgrade with the same variable and `./start.sh pull`. [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr) is one such host. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`.

```bash
MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh
```

Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP.

For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP.

### Try it without an API key

New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate:

1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**.
2. Click **Run SOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step.
3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact.

### What you need for real work

| I want to… | You need |
| --- | --- |
| Run the script + approval demo | Nothing |
| Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor |
| Change an existing repository (in chat or via an SOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |

<details>
<summary><b>More setup details</b>: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model</summary>

<br>

- **Executors.** Pick **CodeBuddy, Codex or Claude Code** beside the home composer, then a model. Each executor uses its own credentials from personal settings, and every SOP role can choose its executor independently (built-in roles default to CodeBuddy). Requirement clarification and AI notification summaries currently use CodeBuddy; scheduled assistant tasks run on the CLI the task selects. The Docker image ships CodeBuddy and Codex; Claude Code installs from npm on first use and is cached, so that first run requires npm access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose.
- **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs.
- **Delivering to a repository.** Choose **Connect GitHub** in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project SOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR.
- **Sandboxes.** In the default Compose installation, SOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See [deployment boundaries](docs/deployment.md#accounts). Re-running the installer keeps your data.
- **Accounts and access.** New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (`AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false` in `.env` turns that off). Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) before exposing it beyond your team.
- **Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers.** See [Deployment](docs/deployment.md).
- **Hacking on LoopForge itself?** `bash scripts/dev.sh` runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).

</details>

## How SOPs work

An **SOP** is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:

<p align="center">
  <picture>
    <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/assets/readme/sop-flow-en-dark.svg">
    <img src="docs/assets/readme/sop-flow-en.svg" alt="The SOP flow: Requirement, then Clarify, Design, Implement, Review (agents), Test (script) and Accept (human gate), then Delivery; acceptance can send work back to Implement" width="100%">
  </picture>
</p>

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/assets/readme/designer-en.svg" alt="The LoopForge SOP designer showing the built-in bug-fix SOP, with the Independent review step selected and its role, executor and failure policy in the inspector" width="100%">
</p>

<p align="center"><sub>The SOP designer with the built-in bug-fix SOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.</sub></p>

| Node | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Agent** | A role (prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools) that designs, implements, reviews or tests. |
| **Script** | A deterministic shell step: build, test, lint, generate a report. No AI where AI is not needed. |
| **Human gate** | Pauses the run until someone checks the artifacts and approves, or sends the work back to a step. |
| **Sub-SOP** | Runs another SOP as a sub-workflow. |
| **Preview build** | Builds a static site and archives it for review. |

Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in SOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/assets/readme/run-approval-en.svg" alt="LoopForge run details: the report script has finished and the run waits at the human gate with approve, add-context and send-back actions" width="100%">
</p>

<p align="center"><sub>A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.</sub></p>

**A delivery we actually ran:** four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The [reusable acceptance case](e2e/api/45-delivery-model.test.mjs) checks the files and results. See the [validation record](docs/validation.md) for scope and known gaps.

## Features

| Area | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| **Chat workbench** | Main Bot with per-conversation executor, model and permission mode. `@` references for roles, skills, requirements, SOPs and repositories. Messages queue while a reply runs; *Steer* interrupts and sends now. Generated files open in a side panel with preview, source and download. |
| **Conversation workspaces** | On-demand Docker sandboxes with the project's repositories checked out, project roles as native subagents, and direct control of a running SOP workspace: pause, resume or take over. |
| **SOP designer** | Visual canvas with Agent, Script, Human gate, Sub-SOP and Preview nodes, rework-on-failure edges, validation, version history and publishing. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. |
| **Roles** | Reusable definitions: prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills, MCP tools, artifacts and gates, shared across SOP nodes and chat subagents. |
| **Requirement → delivery** | Requirements tracked end to end, whether shipped by an SOP or straight from chat, with PR/MR status tracking, merge detection and direct-branch merges. |
| **Runs & approvals** | Live node status, tool traces, worker logs, per-node artifact snapshots and workspace previews. A single **Needs review** inbox for every gate waiting on you. |
| **AI scheduled tasks** | Recurring agent tasks with full workspace, SOP and MCP access; a shared market of versioned, parameterized task templates; automatic SOP dispatch for new requirements. |
| **Insights & cost** | Engineering metrics, business-domain reports with static HTML/SVG export, and token/cost accounting for SOPs and conversations at public list prices. |
| **Execution environments** | Platform workers, Docker sandboxes, or a connected local execution machine using your own tools and repositories. |
| **Team-ready** | Password accounts, projects and members, light/dark/system themes, an OpenAPI-described HTTP and MCP API. Management pages are in English and Chinese; the chat workbench is Chinese for now. |

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/assets/readme/sops-en.svg" alt="The Templates page listing the four built-in SOPs: backend delivery, frontend delivery, product proposal and bug fix" width="100%">
</p>

<p align="center"><sub>Built-in SOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.</sub></p>

## LoopForge Local

Don't want to run a server? **LoopForge Local** brings the built-in delivery workflows straight into the coding assistant you already use:

```bash
# Run inside your target project, e.g. for Claude Code
npx -y loopforge-cli@latest install claude
```

Then run `/start-devflow "<your request>"` in Claude Code.

| Host | Supported |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code · CodeBuddy · Codex · Cursor | Classic (default) and Portable editions |
| Pi | Portable edition |
| DeepSeek Harness | Portable edition |
| Hermes Agent | Portable edition |

See the [local guide](docs/local/usage.md) for each host's entry point and [editions](docs/local/editions.md) for the differences. Source lives in [`local/`](local/). Local runs the built-in workflows today; exporting a platform SOP for standalone local execution is planned.

| | Platform | Local |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Teams sharing chat workspaces, SOPs, approvals and history | One developer inside an IDE or CLI |
| Needs | Docker + Python 3 | Node.js 20+, Python 3.8+ and a coding assistant |
| Workflows | Chat with Main Bot + custom SOPs on a visual canvas | Built-in Classic / Portable workflows |
| Evidence | Shared run details, approvals and metrics in the web workspace | Artifacts under `artifacts/{task_slug}/` + optional local dashboard |

## FAQ

**Do I need an API key to try it?**
No. The demo SOP uses only a script and a human gate. Chat and agent steps need a key for the executor you pick. Model usage is not included; you bring your own credentials.

**Do I need GitHub?**
No. Chat, documents and new projects run in the task workspace. Connect GitHub when you want to change an existing repository or open PRs.

**Should I use chat or an SOP?**
Use chat to explore and iterate; Main Bot can still open a PR. Once you find a way of working you want every requirement to follow, with fixed reviewers, tests and sign-off, put it in an SOP. Main Bot can start, pause and take over SOP runs, so the two paths work together.

**How is this different from Dify, n8n or Flowise?**
Those are general-purpose AI and automation workflow builders. LoopForge is built for **software delivery with coding agents**: implementer and reviewer roles, Docker sandboxes with real repositories, GitHub delivery, human acceptance gates and run evidence.

**How is this different from using Claude Code, Codex or CodeBuddy directly?**
LoopForge doesn't replace them; it orchestrates them. Each agent step and each chat turn runs one of those CLIs. LoopForge adds what surrounds it: who does what, in which sandbox, in which order, with which checks, and who signs off.

**Is it safe to expose on the internet?**
New installations listen on all interfaces and target a trusted team. Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) and set up HTTPS before opening it up. Report vulnerabilities privately via the [security policy](SECURITY.md).

[![Codecov](https://img.shields.io/codecov/c/github/moby/buildkit?logo=codecov&style=flat-square)](https://codecov.io/gh/moby/buildkit)

BuildKit is a toolkit for converting source code to build artifacts in an efficient, expressive and repeatable manner.

Key features:

-   Automatic garbage collection
-   Extendable frontend formats
-   Concurrent dependency resolution
-   Efficient instruction caching
-   Build cache import/export
-   Nested build job invocations
-   Distributable workers
-   Multiple output formats
-   Pluggable architecture
-   Execution without root privileges

Read the proposal from https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/32925

Introductory blog post https://blog.mobyproject.org/introducing-buildkit-17e056cc5317

Join `#buildkit` channel on [Docker Community Slack](https://dockr.ly/comm-slack)

> [!NOTE]

> like `RUN --mount=type=(bind|cache|tmpfs|secret|ssh)`, please refer to the
> [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/).

> [!NOTE]
> `docker build` [uses Buildx and BuildKit by default](https://docs.docker.com/build/architecture/) since Docker Engine 23.0.

## Quick start

:information_source: For Kubernetes deployments, see [`examples/kubernetes`](./examples/kubernetes).

BuildKit is composed of the `buildkitd` daemon and the `buildctl` client.
While the `buildctl` client is available for Linux, macOS, and Windows, the `buildkitd` daemon is only available for Linux and *Windows currently.

The latest binaries of BuildKit are available [here](https://github.com/moby/buildkit/releases) for Linux, macOS, and Windows.


### Linux Setup

The `buildkitd` daemon requires the following components to be installed:
-   [runc](https://github.com/opencontainers/runc) or [crun](https://github.com/containers/crun)
-   [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd) (if you want to use containerd worker)

**Starting the `buildkitd` daemon:**
You need to run `buildkitd` as the root user on the host.

```bash
$ sudo buildkitd
```

To run `buildkitd` as a non-root user, see [`docs/rootless.md`](docs/rootless.md).

The buildkitd daemon supports two worker backends: OCI (runc) and containerd.

By default, the OCI (runc) worker is used. You can set `--oci-worker=false --containerd-worker=true` to use the containerd worker.

We are open to adding more backends.

To start the buildkitd daemon using systemd socket activation, you can install the buildkit systemd unit files.
See [Systemd socket activation](#systemd-socket-activation)

The buildkitd daemon listens gRPC API on `/run/buildkit/buildkitd.sock` by default, but you can also use TCP sockets.
See [Expose BuildKit as a TCP service](#expose-buildkit-as-a-tcp-service).

### Windows Setup

See instructions and notes at [`docs/windows.md`](./docs/windows.md).

### macOS Setup

[Homebrew formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/buildkit) (unofficial) is available for macOS.
```console
$ brew install buildkit
```

The Homebrew formula does not contain the daemon (`buildkitd`).

For example, [Lima](https://lima-vm.io) can be used for launching the daemon inside a Linux VM.
```console
brew install lima
limactl start template://buildkit
export BUILDKIT_HOST="unix://$HOME/.lima/buildkit/sock/buildkitd.sock"
```

### Build from source

To build BuildKit from source, see [`.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`](./.github/CONTRIBUTING.md).

For a `buildctl` reference, see [this document](./docs/reference/buildctl.md).

### Exploring LLB

BuildKit builds are based on a binary intermediate format called LLB that is
used for defining the dependency graph for processes running part of your build.
tl;dr: LLB is to Dockerfile what LLVM IR is to C.

-   Marshaled as Protobuf messages
-   Concurrently executable
-   Efficiently cacheable
-   Vendor-neutral (i.e. non-Dockerfile languages can be easily implemented)

See [`solver/pb/ops.proto`](./solver/pb/ops.proto) for the format definition,
and see [`./examples/README.md`](./examples/README.md) for example LLB
applications.

### Frontends

BuildKit supports different build languages through frontends that translate
build definitions into LLB. The following frontends and tools provide alternatives
for defining builds:

| Project                                                                                                  | Description                                                                          |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [Dockerfile](#exploring-dockerfiles)                                                                     | Build container images using Dockerfile instructions.                                |
| [Buildpacks](https://github.com/tonistiigi/buildkit-pack)                                                | Build applications using buildpacks.                                                 |
| [Mockerfile](https://mattrickard.com/building-a-new-dockerfile-frontend/)                                | Example YAML frontend for Ubuntu packages and external dependencies.                 |
| [Gockerfile](https://github.com/po3rin/gockerfile)                                                       | Build simple Go servers from YAML definitions.                                       |
| [bldr (Pkgfile)](https://github.com/siderolabs/bldr)                                                     | Build and package software distributions using YAML definitions.                     |
| [HLB](https://github.com/openllb/hlb)                                                                    | Define builds as containerized units of work in a high-level build language.         |
| [Earthfile (Earthly)](https://github.com/earthly/earthly)                                                | Define repeatable builds with Dockerfile-like syntax. No longer actively maintained. |
| [Cargo Wharf (Rust)](https://github.com/denzp/cargo-wharf)                                               | Build Rust container images from Cargo build plans with per-dependency caching.      |
| [Nix](https://github.com/reproducible-containers/buildkit-nix)                                           | Build container images from Nix derivations and flakes.                              |
| [mopy (Python)](https://github.com/cmdjulian/mopy)                                                       | Package Python applications into container images using YAML definitions.            |
| [envd (Starlark)](https://github.com/tensorchord/envd)                                                   | Define container-based development environments for AI/ML.                           |
| [Blubber](https://gitlab.wikimedia.org/repos/releng/blubber)                                             | Build application container images from declarative YAML.                            |
| [Bass](https://github.com/vito/bass)                                                                     | Script builds and project infrastructure with a Lisp dialect.                        |
| [kraft.yaml (Unikraft)](https://github.com/unikraft/kraftkit/tree/staging/tools/dockerfile-llb-frontend) | Build Unikraft unikernel images from Kraftfiles.                                     |
| [Massé](https://github.com/marxarelli/masse)                                                             | Define composable container image build graphs in CUE.                               |
| [DALEC](https://github.com/project-dalec/dalec)                                                          | Build system packages and container images from declarative specifications.          |
| [Dexfile](https://github.com/dexnore/dexfile)                                                            | Extend Dockerfile syntax with conditions, loops, imports, and functions.             |
| [Docker Sandbox Kit](https://github.com/docker/sandbox-kit-spec)                                         | Build Docker Sandbox kits from YAML descriptors.                                     |

Open a pull request to add your own frontend or build language.

### Exploring Dockerfiles

Frontends are components that run inside BuildKit and convert any build definition to LLB. There is a special frontend called gateway (`gateway.v0`) that allows using any image as a frontend.

During development, Dockerfile frontend (`dockerfile.v0`) is also part of the BuildKit repo. In the future, this will be moved out, and Dockerfiles can be built using an external image.

#### Building a Dockerfile with `buildctl`

```bash
buildctl build \
    --frontend=dockerfile.v0 \
    --local context=. \
    --local dockerfile=.
# or
buildctl build \
    --frontend=dockerfile.v0 \
    --local context=. \
    --local dockerfile=. \
    --opt target=foo \
    --opt build-arg:foo=bar
```

`--local` exposes local source files from client to the builder. `context` and `dockerfile` are the names Dockerfile frontend looks for build context and Dockerfile location.

If the Dockerfile has a different filename it can be specified with `--opt filename=./Dockerfile-alternative`.

#### Building a Dockerfile using external frontend

External versions of the Dockerfile frontend are pushed to https://hub.docker.com/r/docker/dockerfile-upstream and https://hub.docker.com/r/docker/dockerfile and can be used with the gateway frontend. The source for the external frontend is currently located in `./frontend/dockerfile/cmd/dockerfile-frontend` but will move out of this repository in the future ([#163](https://github.com/moby/buildkit/issues/163)). For automatic build from master branch of this repository `docker/dockerfile-upstream:master` or `docker/dockerfile-upstream:master-labs` image can be used.

```bash
buildctl build \
    --frontend gateway.v0 \
    --opt source=docker/dockerfile \
    --local context=. \
    --local dockerfile=.
buildctl build \
    --frontend gateway.v0 \
    --opt source=docker/dockerfile \
    --opt context=https://github.com/moby/moby.git \
    --opt build-arg:APT_MIRROR=cdn-fastly.deb.debian.org
```

### Output

By default, the build result and intermediate cache will only remain internally in BuildKit. An output needs to be specified to retrieve the result.

#### Image/Registry

```bash
buildctl build ... --output type=image,name=docker.io/username/image,push=true
```

To export the image to multiple registries:

```bash
buildctl build ... --output type=image,\"name=docker.io/username/image,docker.io/username2/image2\",push=true
```

To export the cache embed with the image and pushing them to registry together, type `registry` is required to import the cache, you should specify `--export-cache type=inline` and `--import-cache type=registry,ref=...`. To export the cache to a local directly, you should specify `--export-cache type=local`.
Details in [Export cache](#export-cache).

```bash
buildctl build ...\
  --output type=image,name=docker.io/username/image,push=true \
  --export-cache type=inline \
  --import-cache type=registry,ref=docker.io/username/image
```

Keys supported by image output:
* `name=<value>`: specify image name(s)
* `push=true`: push after creating the image
* `push-by-digest=true`: push unnamed image
* `registry.insecure=true`: push to insecure HTTP registry
* `oci-mediatypes=<true|false>`: use OCI media types for image manifests, indexes and configuration JSON instead of Docker's.
  See [media type defaults and attestation requirements](docs/build-repro.md#compatibility-version).
* `oci-artifact=true`: use OCI artifact format for attestations when OCI media types are enabled. Set to `false` to use the legacy attestation image manifest format.
* `unpack=true`: unpack image after creation (for use with containerd)
* `dangling-name-prefix=<value>`: name image with `prefix@<digest>`, used for anonymous images
* `name-canonical=true`: add additional canonical name `name@<digest>`
* `compression=<uncompressed|gzip|estargz|zstd>`: choose compression type for layers newly created and cached, gzip is default value. estargz should be used with `oci-mediatypes=true`.
* `compression-level=<value>`: compression level for gzip, estargz (0-9) and zstd (0-22)
* `rewrite-timestamp=true`: rewrite the file timestamps to the `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` value.
   See [`docs/build-repro.md`](docs/build-repro.md) for how to specify the `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` value.
* `force-compression=true`: forcefully apply `compression` option to all layers (including already existing layers)
* `store=true`: store the result images to the worker's (e.g. containerd) image store as well as ensures that the image has all blobs in the content store (default `true`). Ignored if the worker doesn't have image store (e.g. OCI worker).
* `annotation.<key>=<value>`: attach an annotation with the respective `key` and `value` to the built image
  * Using the extended syntaxes, `annotation-<type>.<key>=<value>`, `annotation[<platform>].<key>=<value>` and both combined with `annotation-<type>[<platform>].<key>=<value>`, allows configuring exactly where to attach the annotation.
  * `<type>` specifies what object to attach to, and can be any of `manifest` (the default), `manifest-descriptor`, `index` and `index-descriptor`
  * `<platform>` specifies which objects to attach to (by default, all), and is the same key passed into the `platform` opt, see [`docs/multi-platform.md`](docs/multi-platform.md).
  * See [`docs/annotations.md`](docs/annotations.md) for more details.

If credentials are required, `buildctl` will attempt to read Docker configuration file `$DOCKER_CONFIG/config.json`.
`$DOCKER_CONFIG` defaults to `~/.docker`.

#### Local directory

The local client will copy the files directly to the client. This is useful if BuildKit is being used for building something else than container images.

```bash
buildctl build ... --output type=local,dest=path/to/output-dir
```

To export specific files use multi-stage builds with a scratch stage and copy the needed files into that stage with `COPY --from`.

```dockerfile
...
FROM scratch as testresult

COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/testresult.xml .
...
```

```bash
buildctl build ... --opt target=testresult --output type=local,dest=path/to/output-dir
```

Alternatively, `src=<path>` exports only part of the build result, without
needing a dedicated stage:

```bash
buildctl build ... --output type=local,dest=path/to/output-dir,src=/usr/src/app/reports
```

The contents of `src` are written to the root of the destination, so
`src=/usr/src/app/reports` exports `reports/index.html` as `index.html`. Omit
`src` to export the entire filesystem.

`src` must point to a directory, and is always resolved from the root of the
build result, so `src=app/build` and `src=/app/build` are equivalent. Symlinks

build, `src` is applied to each platform.

Use a BuildKit daemon that supports `src`. Older daemons ignore unknown exporter
options and may export the entire build result instead.

# Agent Substrate

**Zero-trust sandboxing for millions of agents on Kubernetes.**

## What is Agent Substrate?

Agent Substrate is a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. Purpose-built for the era of autonomous agents, Substrate delivers fast resume operations in less than 500ms, with more than 500 activations per second. Agents get isolated compute, identity, networking, and storage. Sensitive credentials are kept out of reach from untrusted code. It supports multiple sandbox technologies, including microVMs and gVisor, while enabling a consistent lifecycle and management of all sandboxes.

At its core, Agent Substrate maps a larger set of “actors” (stateful workloads such as agents) onto a smaller pool of ready “workers”. Because agents spend most of their lives waiting on models, tools, or humans, Substrate snapshots idle actors out of memory and restores them when a request arrives.

Substrate is a low-opinion runtime, not an agent SDK. The workloads it runs do not have to be AI agents, though autonomous, untrusted, mostly-idle agents are the target for its isolation and scheduling model. It runs on standard Kubernetes: Pods, autoscaling, NetworkPolicies. It adds agent-specific scheduling, snapshotting, identity, and network mediation. This allows agentic, inference, training, and reinforcement learning workloads to share one infrastructure plane.

## Security Model

Substrate treats every actor as untrusted and mutually hostile, so tenants can share physical nodes without sharing a security boundary. Every control operates within the cold-start and resume budget. See the [Security Guide](docs/security/security.md) for the full list of security principles and threat model.

* **Always sandboxed, VM-grade boundaries:** Every actor runs inside a dedicated [gVisor](https://gvisor.dev/) (`runsc`) or [Cloud Hypervisor](https://www.cloudhypervisor.org/) microVM sandbox with segregated compute, network, and storage. Plain Linux containers are not supported.
* **Per-agent cryptographic identity:** Every active actor receives a short-lived [SPIFFE](https://spiffe.io/) X.509 certificate by default, and the egress gateway can mint per-actor JWTs on demand when an egress policy calls for one. Both carry the actor identity and atespace (the Substrate namespace grouping), and are designed to federate with external identity systems.
* **Zero credentials in the sandbox:** Actors never hold actor identity JWTs/certs, API keys, or cloud tokens. The built-in egress gateway ([`atenet-egress`](docs/guides/egress-credential-injection.md)) injects credentials into approved outbound requests outside the sandbox, so a prompt-injected or compromised agent has nothing to exfiltrate.
* **Default-deny networking:** Actors start with a private network stack, no inbound path except through the ingress router (`atenet-router`), no lateral actor-to-actor or control-plane access, and outbound traffic [restricted by the egress gateway](docs/guides/egress-traffic.md).
* **Pluggable policy at the edge:** The egress gateway acts as an external Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that is fully replaceable, allowing you to attach your own authorization, DLP, prompt-injection scanning, or cloud IAM policy engine without placing policy code inside the untrusted sandbox.

## Performance & Multiplexing

[![Agent Substrate Demo](https://img.youtube.com/vi/ZEzkCFJkzjY/hq1.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZEzkCFJkzjY)

*Watch the Agent Substrate cluster multiplex ~250 stateful actors across just 8 physical pods.*

This demo highlights the core developer experience and "Agentic Infrastructure" capabilities of Substrate:

1. **Actor Teleport:** Suspend and resume actors onto any available worker in the pool, when needed.
2. **Full-State Persistence:** Working memory (RAM) and filesystem state are captured in snapshots and restored intact across hibernation cycles, without losing in-flight sessions or tool state.
3. **10x–30x Oversubscription:** Multiplex a large registry of stateful actors onto a small pool of warm worker pods, paying for compute only while an agent is actively thinking or executing a tool.

To reproduce this demo in your own cluster, see the **[Counter Demo](demos/counter/README.md)**. For more walkthroughs, visit the **[agent-substrate YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCN9PPqlTtVxlcpbQ-NWpfZQ)**.

## Star History

<a href="https://www.star-history.com/?repos=agent-substrate%2Fsubstrate&type=date&legend=top-left">

    <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=agent-substrate/substrate&type=date&theme=dark&legend=top-left">

## Framework Agnostic & Compatibility

Agent Substrate is **framework and agent harness agnostic**. Because it runs standard OCI container images inside gVisor or microVM sandboxes and enforces security outside the workload, it hosts agents built on any stack without SDK changes:

* **Agent Development Kit (ADK):** Preserves session state across invocations as actor state.
* **LangChain:** Drop-in execution environment for LangChain agents and tool calls.
* **Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity:** High-density, stateful coding environments that keep system and filesystem state across sessions while isolating untrusted code execution.
* **Model Context Protocol (MCP):** Deploy sandboxed MCP servers as Substrate Actors with per-actor identity and egress controls.

## Ecosystem & Examples

*   **[Agent Executor](https://github.com/google/ax):** A distributed agent runtime that demonstrates building a secure, hyper-scalable agent harness on Agent Substrate (see the [announcement blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/agent-executor-googles-distributed-agent-runtime) and [integration guide](https://github.com/google/ax#2-deploy-the-control-plane)).
*   **[kagent](https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent):** A CNCF Sandbox project and Kubernetes-native framework for building, deploying, and managing AI agents that uses Agent Substrate to run sandboxed, stateful agent workloads (see the [announcement blog](https://kagent.dev/blog/the-future-of-kagent)).

## Status and compatibility

Agent Substrate has reached 1.0. We are committed to compatibility and stability of the public API, CLI, and configuration formats. We will continue to add new features, but we will not break existing APIs or configuration formats without a major version bump. See "Compatibility and schema evolution" in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for more details.

### Supported Kubernetes Releases

Currently we aim to support the [latest stable release](https://kubernetes.io/releases/) of Kubernetes, and the previous minor release.

## Community

For announcements, technical discussions, and community support, please join
the **[ate-dev](https://groups.google.com/g/ate-dev)** Google Group.

We host a weekly community meeting every Thursday from 10:00am - 11:00am PST.
- Video call link: https://meet.google.com/uhq-cxvn-dhy
- Or dial: (US) +1 253-289-6971 PIN: 787 664 574 59#
- More phone numbers: https://tel.meet/uhq-cxvn-dhy?pin=9044088223662
- [Meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1obSIvfcafLNniLYTQCcT2eCgxHqa2AQ3Ga7YTsju49s) for the weekly sync meeting
- [Recordings and transcripts](https://drive.google.com/corp/drive/u/0/folders/1rX1S6vPxPrR8dA1lEBuBEXkGKjHtG-mL) of all community meetings

We also have channels in the CNCF slack; [request an invite here](https://slack.cncf.io/)
if you don't have access.

- [#substrate-users](https://cloud-native.slack.com/archives/C0B6RCAJULW) to discuss using substrate.
- [#substrate-dev](https://cloud-native.slack.com/archives/C0B6M3E2J3D) to discuss developing substrate.

## Developing

Please see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for guidelines on contributing to
the project.  We welcome contributions of all kinds, but the project is VERY
young.  Our immediate focus is on building out the core system and demos, so we
may not be able to review or merge contributions that don't align with those
goals in the near term.

## Quickstart (Development)

To quickly set up the complete environment:

1. Make sure you have [Go](https://go.dev/doc/install), [`kubectl`](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/), and [`docker`](https://www.docker.com/) installed and configured on your dev machine. We will automatically manage other dependencies via Go, including [`kind`](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/).
   A Linux host that will run more than about a thousand sandboxes also needs a larger kernel neighbor table (`net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1/2/3` = 4096/16384/32768); `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh` warns when the host is at the default of 1024.

2. Run the following steps:
```shell
# create cluster and local registry
hack/create-kind-cluster.sh

# make ate-setup target the kind cluster; set this in every shell that runs
# ate-setup, including for the demo walkthroughs
export ATE_INSTALL_KIND=true

# install Substrate
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy ate-system --credential-provider='{"name":"k8s.io"}' \
  --ingress-allowed-spiffe-ids=spiffe://cluster.local/ns/ate-system/sa/atenet-client

# install counter demo
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy demo counter

# install kubectl-ate
go install ./cmd/kubectl-ate

# create a counter actor in the demo's atespace (--template names the
# actor template, resolved in the actor's atespace)
kubectl ate create actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter --template counter

# serve a local proxy on port 8000 that sends requests to the actor through the
# network router
kubectl ate proxy actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `{"name":"k8s.io"}` deploys the bundled credential provider with an empty,
> default-deny namespace policy. Before an actor can have a credential
> injected, grant its atespace the namespaces whose Secrets it may read; see
> [Enable it](docs/guides/egress-credential-injection.md#enable-it).

3. In a **separate terminal**, send an HTTP request to increment the counter:
```shell
curl -X POST -i http://localhost:8000/
```

### Custom Setup and Deployment

You can deploy or cleanup specific Agent Substrate components using
the installation script. See `go run ./cmd/ate-setup` for all options.
```bash
# Re-deploy only ate-apiserver of the ATE system
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy apiserver

# Delete everything (core system and all demos)
go run ./cmd/ate-setup delete all
```

### Tearing down local `kind` resources

If you need to delete the local `kind` cluster and its registry (if it was created by `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh`):

```bash
./hack/delete-kind-cluster.sh
```

### GKE Quickstart

To deploy on Google Kubernetes Engine, follow the official
[GKE Installation Guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/ai-ml/install-overview-substrate).
It lists the prerequisites and gives the one-line installer command. The
installer's source and detailed options are in
[substrate-gke](https://github.com/ai-on-gke/substrate-gke).

## Demos

We provide several sample applications demonstrating Agent Substrate's capabilities:

1. **[Counter Demo](demos/counter/README.md)**: A stateful Go HTTP server demonstrating state preservation across suspends/resumes, and on-demand actor resumption and routing via the Substrate router.
2. **[Sandbox Demo (Antigravity)](demos/sandbox/README.md)**: A secure, sandboxed execution environment (running Alpine Linux) that allows arbitrary shell execution while preserving filesystem state across sessions.
3. **[Claude Code Multiplex](demos/claude-code-multiplex/README.md)**: Demonstrates oversubscribing physical hardware by multiplexing multiple Claude Code agents onto a limited pool of workers.
4. **[Multi-Template](demos/multi-template/README.md)**: Two `ActorTemplate`s running different binaries share one `WorkerPool`, even though the templates live in different atespaces.
5. **[Request Parking](demos/parking/README.md)**: An oversubscribed pool where the router holds inbound requests until a worker frees up, instead of returning `503`.

### Documentation & Guides
* [Architecture](docs/concepts/architecture.md): How the control plane, node supervisor, and networking stack fit together.
* [API Configuration Guide](docs/reference/api-guide.md): Detailed reference for configuring WorkerPools, ActorTemplates, Secrets, and Volumes.
* [Full CLI Documentation](docs/reference/kubectl-ate.md): Installation and usage for `kubectl-ate`.
* [Glossary](docs/reference/glossary.md): Core terms (Actor, Atespace, ActorTemplate, WorkerPool, Worker, ate-api-server, atenet, atelet, ateworker) and how they relate.
* [Integration Repositories](docs/project/integration-repos.md): Where integrations live, how their repositories are named, and how fixes flow back to core.
* [Observability Guide](docs/guides/observability.md): Guide to actor logging, metrics, and distributed tracing.
* [Extending Substrate](docs/security/extensibility.md): How to augment or replace the built-in ingress and egress gateways.
* [Authentication Guide](docs/guides/authentication.md): Which credential people, pods and CI jobs should use with the Substrate API, and how to trust more JWT issuers.
* [Actor JWTs](docs/guides/actor-jwts.md): What an actor JWT contains, how relying parties verify it, and how to rotate the signing key.
* [Federating actor JWTs](docs/guides/actor-jwt-federation.md): Serve the actor JWT issuer publicly and set up a relying party outside the cluster to trust it.
* [Rotating the actor JWT signing key](docs/guides/actor-jwt-key-rotation.md): The rotation steps, how long to wait between them, and replacing a compromised key.
* [Egress Traffic](docs/guides/egress-traffic.md): Which protocols an Actor may reach the outside world with and which are blocked.
* [Enabling man-in-the-middle (MITM) interception for Actor Egress policy](docs/guides/egress-trust-bundle.md): Egress policies such as header injection depend on MITM interception of Actor traffic. This guide explains how an Actor should be configured to enable interception.

## Tour

### Commands

* `cmd/ateworker-gvisor`: An interior-pod helper running inside sandboxed worker pods to execute `runsc` checkpoint and restore commands.
* `cmd/ateworker-microvm`: The microVM peer of `ateworker-gvisor`, running actors as cloud-hypervisor VMs.

* `cmd/benchmarking`: Synthetic workloads used by the load tests, including `glutton`, which consumes RAM, disk, and file descriptors on demand.

like netcat, but over Tailscale's data plane, without Tailscale's control plane

Language: Go

Stars: 9,069

README

<p align="center">
  <img src="tailcat.png" alt="Tailcat" width="149" height="176">
</p>

<p align="center"><em>"Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale"</em></p>

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/tailscale/tailcat"><img src="https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/tailscale/tailcat.svg" alt="Go Reference"></a>
  <a href="https://bsky.app/profile/tailcat.dev"><img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/Bluesky-@tailcat.dev-0285FF?logo=bluesky&logoColor=white" alt="Follow @tailcat.dev on Bluesky"></a>
</p>

# Tailcat

Tailcat is a remix of Tailscale open source pieces to act like
[netcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netcat), but over Tailscale's data plane,
without Tailscale's control plane. Tailscale's data plane (`magicsock`,
internally) gives you point-to-point WireGuard®-encrypted tunnels between two
machines with DERP as the NAT-hole-punching communication side channel and the
ultimate relay-of-last-resort if NAT traversal fails. Instead of using the
Tailscale control plane, all `tailcat` connection metadata is exchanged out of
band, however you want.

The `tailcat` CLI (in `cmd/tailcat`) is built on the `tailcat` Go library
(importable as [`github.com/tailscale/tailcat`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/tailscale/tailcat)).

Whether you use `tailcat` as a CLI tool or library, one side runs a `tailcat`
server (listener) and gets back a short tailcat address. The other side passes
that tailcat address to `tailcat`'s client side to connect. All traffic between
the two is
encrypted end-to-end with WireGuard. The initial connection bootstraps through
a DERP server ([see below](#bring-your-own-derp-relay)), and then magicsock performs NAT traversal to
upgrade to a direct peer-to-peer UDP connection when possible (usually!).

You don't need a Tailscale account, root/admin access on the machine
(it doesn't alter your machine's routing tables, DNS, etc.). It's just
a userspace library and CLI tool.

And it's all open source.

You can use our free rate-limited DERP relays (the default DERP map is
https://tailcat.dev/derpmap.json) or you can [run your own](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/tree/main/cmd/derper#derp).

There's also an experimental in-browser web demo (tailcat compiled to
WebAssembly) at https://tailscale.github.io/tailcat/ that can send and
receive files or text, interoperating with the CLI. Browser traffic is
relayed over DERP only, with no direct connections until WebRTC
support ([#4](https://github.com/tailscale/tailcat/issues/4)).

## Install

See [INSTALL.md](./INSTALL.md) for details on each, including notes
for packagers building from source:

| Method | Linux | macOS | Windows | FreeBSD,<br>OpenBSD | Browser<br>(js/wasm) |
|--------|:-----:|:-----:|:-------:|:-------------------:|:--------------------:|
| [Static binaries](INSTALL.md#prebuilt-binaries) | ✅ | | ✅ | | |
| [.deb packages](INSTALL.md#prebuilt-binaries) | Debian, Ubuntu, ... | | | | |
| [.rpm packages](INSTALL.md#prebuilt-binaries) | Red Hat, Fedora, ... | | | | |
| [Homebrew](INSTALL.md#homebrew-macos) | | ✅ | | | |
| [Scoop](INSTALL.md#scoop-windows) | | | ✅ | | |
| [Snap](INSTALL.md#snap-linux) | ✅ | | | | |
| [Container image](INSTALL.md#container-image) | ✅ | | | | |
| [Nix](INSTALL.md#nix) | ✅ | ✅ | | | |
| [AUR](INSTALL.md#arch-linux-aur) | Arch | | | | |
| [conda-forge](INSTALL.md#conda-forge) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | |
| [Build from source](INSTALL.md#go-toolchain) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Usage

### Pipe stdin/stdout between two machines

Server starts, printing out its ephemeral address:
```sh
$ tailcat
# Selected bootstrap relay region 302, San Francisco
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
(hangs, waiting...)
```

And then the client can:

```sh
$ echo hello | tailcat tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
$ 
```

Then the server unblocks:

```sh
$ tailcat
# Selected bootstrap relay region 302, San Francisco
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
hello
$
```

### Expose local ports through the tunnel

Or you can serve a local TCP port, forwarded to localhost:

```sh
$ tailcat serve 8080,8443 # or: tailcat serve all
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

And then the client:

```sh
$ tailcat tcXXXXXXXXX 8080
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: foo

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
....
```

A port mapping proxies a port somewhere other than the same port on localhost: to a different local port, or to a host and port elsewhere on the server's network. This serves port 5555 by proxying it to an Android device's adb port on the LAN, without exposing the rest of the network the way `exit-node` would:

```sh
$ tailcat serve 5555:10.2.200.213:5555
# Proxying port 5555 to 10.2.200.213:5555
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

Then on the client, `tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX 5555` followed by `adb connect 127.0.0.1:5555`. Write IPv6 targets in brackets: `5555:[fd7a::1]:5555`.

### Forward local ports to a tailcat server

To make ports served by a tailcat server available as ordinary local TCP ports (for browsers, database clients, or other tools that do not support SOCKS or stdio), run `forward` with the server's tailcat address:

```sh
$ tailcat serve 8080,3306
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX 18080:8080 3306
```

A local port of 0 asks the operating system for a free port; each listener prints its address once it's listening.

To forward local ports to assets on the network reachable by an exit-node server, run the server in exit-node mode and specify each remote IP address and port in the mapping:

```sh
$ tailcat serve exit-node
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX \
    3001:172.23.52.30:3001 \
    17170:172.23.52.31:17170
```

This forwards `127.0.0.1:3001` to `172.23.52.30:3001` and `127.0.0.1:17170` to `172.23.52.31:17170` through the exit-node server.

By default, listeners bind to `127.0.0.1` and diagnostic logs are suppressed. Pass `--verbose` before the subcommand to enable verbose networking logs. Use `--bind=0.0.0.0` only when clients on other machines should be able to connect:

```sh
$ tailcat forward --bind=0.0.0.0 tcXXXXXXXXX 18080:8080
```

Press Ctrl-C to stop forwarding.

### Open a browser to a tailcat server

To view a web server behind a tailcat server, run `browse`:

```sh
$ tailcat serve 80
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat browse tcXXXXXXXXX
```

This is an alias for `tailcat forward --open-browser <tc-addr> 0:80`: it opens `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` in a web browser once the local listener is ready, then blocks, forwarding connections, until interrupted. The `--open-browser` flag works with any single `forward` port mapping.

### Public-key-authenticated SSH server

Run an SSH server that accepts keys from local `authorized_keys` files,
literal OpenSSH public key lines, or GitHub accounts:

```sh
$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=~/.ssh/authorized_keys ssh
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

Multiple sources can be comma-separated. A `user@github` source fetches
`https://github.com/user.keys` once, before the server starts:

```sh
$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=bradfitz@github,./contractor.pub ssh
```

Every source must exist, fetch successfully, and contain valid public key
lines or startup fails. Authorized-key options such as `command=` and
`from=` are rejected because the built-in server does not implement them.
Running `tailcat serve ssh` without `--ssh-authorized-keys` also fails; use the
explicit `no-auth-ssh` service when the tunnel identity alone is sufficient.

### Auth-free SSH server

On Linux, macOS, and Windows, you can also explicitly run the SSH server with
no client authentication. The encrypted tunnel provides the client identity.

```sh
$ tailcat serve no-auth-ssh
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

> [!WARNING]
> With `no-auth-ssh`, the address **is** the credential: anyone who
> learns it gets a shell as the user running the server. Share it only
> over private channels, and never publish it, in a DNS TXT record or
> anywhere else public. If you want an SSH server reachable by DNS
> name, it must require client authentication: `--allow` at the tunnel
> layer, `--ssh-authorized-keys` at the SSH layer, or both.

And on the client side:

```sh
$ tailcat ssh tcXXXXXXXXX
$ tailcat ssh tcXXXXXXXXX ls -la
```

### Run a command per connection

Like inetd, the `exec` service runs a command for each incoming
connection, with the connection as the command's stdin and stdout.
The command comes after `--`:

```sh
$ tailcat serve exec -- /usr/bin/fortune
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

```sh
$ tailcat tcXXXXXXXXX 80 < /dev/null
```

The command's stderr goes to the server's. It gets the peer's node
key in `$TAILCAT_PEER_KEY` (in `--allow`'s format) and the peer's
tailcat IP:port in `$TAILCAT_REMOTE_ADDR`.

Given with the `ssh` or `no-auth-ssh` service, the command instead
replaces the shell, like OpenSSH's `ForceCommand`: every SSH session
runs only that command (on a PTY if the client asks for one), and the
server offers no shell, no client-chosen command, and no SFTP. The
client's requested command, if any, arrives in `$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`.

```sh
$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=alice@github ssh -- ./deploy.sh
$ tailcat serve no-auth-ssh -- git-upload-pack /srv/repo.git
```

### Send and receive files

To receive files, run a drop box and share the printed tailcat address:

```sh
$ tailcat recv ~/inbox
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

The sender then runs:

```sh
$ tailcat cp report.pdf tcXXXXXXXXX:
```

`tailcat cp` runs the system `scp` with the connection routed through
tailcat, so you get its usual progress display, and `-r` for
directory trees. The drop box is write-only: senders can't list the
directory, read anything back, or touch existing files.

To offer files instead, serve a directory read-only (the default) or
read-write:

```sh
$ tailcat serve files                  # current directory, read-only
$ tailcat serve --files=/pub:rw files  # a given directory, read-write
```

```sh
$ tailcat ls -l tcXXXXXXXXX
$ tailcat cp tcXXXXXXXXX:report.pdf .
```

`tailcat ls` speaks SFTP natively, so it works even without OpenSSH
installed.

The server confines all paths to the served directory (via Go's
`os.Root`), so neither `..` nor symlinks escape it. The file service
speaks SFTP, so the stock `sftp` and `scp` clients also work against
it, given a ProxyCommand that pipes through tailcat (the same trick
`tailcat cp` and `tailcat ssh` use). Both `ssh` and `no-auth-ssh`
servers serve SFTP too, with the same access as the shell.

Transfers are not compressed: the SFTP protocol has no compression
of its own, and the SSH transport here doesn't either (Go's SSH
stack omits it; transport compression has a history of security
problems, and TLS dropped it too). Compress files before sending
if it matters.

### Measure throughput and latency

Run an iperf-like test between two machines. The server accepts tests
with the `perf` service and the client sends to it for 10 seconds by
default, printing progress each second and both sides' totals at the
end. `--reverse` sends the other way, `--bidir` both ways at once,
`--udp` tests UDP (paced to `--bitrate`, default 1 Mbit/s) and reports
loss, reordering, and jitter, and `--parallel` runs several streams.
Round trips over the test's control connection measure latency while
the tunnel is loaded:

```sh
$ tailcat serve perf
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

```sh
$ tailcat perf tcXXXXXXXXX
# path: direct via 203.0.113.7:41641, rtt 1.2ms
TCP, client -> server, 1 stream, 10s
[   1.0s]  sent    118 MB    943 Mbit/s  rtt 2.1ms
...
sent        1.18 GB in   10.0s    943 Mbit/s
received    1.18 GB in   10.0s    942 Mbit/s
rtt under load  min 1.9ms  avg 2.3ms  max 4.1ms  (50 samples)
```

The test first waits for a direct path (up to `--timeout`) and refuses
to run through a DERP relay otherwise, since a throughput test through
a shared relay mostly measures its rate limit while crowding out
everyone else. `--via-derp` allows a relayed test through [a relay you
run yourself](#bring-your-own-derp-relay); Tailscale's shared relays
are always refused. `tailcat --json perf` prints the results as JSON.

### Misc commands 

Ping to test connectivity; each pong reports whether it arrived via a
DERP relay or a direct path. `--until-direct` keeps pinging (up to
`--timeout`, default 10s) until a direct path works, exiting non-zero
if one doesn't:

```sh
$ tailcat ping --until-direct <tc-addr>
pong in 42.1ms via DERP(sfo)
pong in 1.2ms via 203.0.113.7:41641
```

Run a command through a SOCKS5 proxy routed over the tunnel:

```sh
$ tailcat socks <tc-addr> curl http://server.tailcat:8081/
```

Tailcat addresses also work directly as URL hostnames: the SOCKS proxy recognizes
and dials them, so the tailcat address argument is optional. (Tailcat addresses are
case-sensitive; this works with curl and most CLI tools, but not with
browsers, which lowercase hostnames.)

```sh
$ tailcat socks curl http://<tc-addr>:8081/
```

Act as an exit node so the client can reach the server's network:

```sh
$ tailcat serve exit-node
```

Parse a tailcat address and print its contents (the server's WireGuard
public key and DERP info) as JSON, without connecting to anything:

```sh
$ tailcat parse tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
{
    "ServerPublic": "nodekey:9c8d2e6728da80a1dd37e275a82595b42d9a838610bc53f74a7670d1610f2e34",
    "RegionID": 302
}
```

Resolve a short tailcat address (which references a DERP region by ID, requiring
clients to fetch the DERP map) into a longer self-contained one with the
DERP server info embedded, letting clients connect more quickly:

```sh
$ tailcat resolve tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu

```

Parsing that resolved tailcat address shows the embedded DERP info:

```sh
$ tailcat parse tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFygaFhToGjYWhudGMzMDJhLmlwbi5kZXZhNG0yMDguMTExLjM5LjM4YTZzMjYwNzpmNzQwOjA6M2Y6OjcyMA
{
    "ServerPublic": "nodekey:9c8d2e6728da80a1dd37e275a82595b42d9a838610bc53f74a7670d1610f2e34",
    "Region": [
        {
            "Nodes": [
                {
                    "HostName": "tc302a.ipn.dev",
                    "IPv4": "208.111.39.38",
                    "IPv6": "2607:f740:0:3f::720"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

A server can print the long self-contained form directly with the
`tailcat serve --full-address` flag.

## Key Management

A server's tailcat address contains its WireGuard public key and an independent
WireGuard pre-shared key, so the saved key material determines who can reach you:

* **Ephemeral keys (the default):** each server run generates a fresh key in
  memory and prints an address nobody has ever seen. When the process exits,
  the key is discarded and the address is dead forever. This is the safe
  default: sharing that address only ever refers to that one run.

* **Saved keys:** `tailcat genkey` generates a key saved to disk so the
  address stays stable across restarts. The flip side: anyone you've *ever*
  shared that address with can connect to any future server using that key,
  unless you restrict clients with `tailcat serve --allow` (see
  `tailcat genkey --client`).

The CLI says at startup which kind it's using, so you know whether you're
starting a fresh single-use server or re-listening on an address you may
have shared in the past.

WireGuard pre-shared keys are enabled by default and strongly recommended. For
compatibility with tailcat clients v0.5.0 and earlier, `--psk=false` on `serve`
or `genkey` produces shorter addresses, but removes post-quantum protection and
protection from public DERP operators that observe the peers' public keys.

```sh
$ tailcat genkey --key=default --region=nyc
# prints the tailcat address; key saved to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/default.private.json

# later; the key named "default" is used automatically once it exists:
$ tailcat serve 8080
# 🐈 Server listening with saved key "default": tcXXXXXXXXX

# ... unless you force a one-off ephemeral key:
$ tailcat serve --key=new 8080
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX
```

That is, `default` is a magic key name: once it exists, plain `tailcat`
silently uses it instead of generating an ephemeral key, and the startup
line above is what tells you which happened. Use `--key=new` to get an
ephemeral key anyway, `--key=<name>` to use a different saved key, or
`tailcat genkey --delete --key=default` to remove the saved default key.
`tailcat genkey --list` lists your saved keys.

Tailcat addresses can also be published as DNS TXT records and looked up by name;
a DNS name works anywhere the CLI takes a tailcat address:

```sh
# If example.com has a TXT record "tailcat=tc..."
$ tailcat example.com 8080
$ tailcat ssh example.com
$ tailcat ping example.com
```

> [!WARNING]
> A tailcat address is normally a secret: knowing it is what lets a
> client connect. A DNS TXT record is **not** secret. It is public,
> world-readable, and actively scanned. Publishing an address in DNS
> hands it to everyone on the internet, so the server behind it must
> authenticate clients by something other than knowledge of the
> address: restrict the tunnel to known client keys with `tailcat
> serve --allow=...`, or, for SSH, require public keys with `tailcat
> serve --ssh-authorized-keys=... ssh`. Never publish the address of a
> `no-auth-ssh` server (or any other server that trusts whoever
> connects): that is a shell on your machine, published in a TXT
> record. See [Protected SSH server over
> DNS](#protected-ssh-server-over-dns) for the safe setup.

## Examples

### Protected SSH server over DNS

Who needs port forwarding or port knocking? This runs an SSH server
reachable from anywhere by name, with no open inbound ports on the
server, where WireGuard authenticates the client before the SSH
server ever sees a packet.

> [!WARNING]
> The `--allow` flag below is not optional decoration. The DNS TXT
> record makes the tailcat address public, so possession of the
> address no longer proves anything: the server must authenticate
> clients itself, here by allowing only one client node key. Without
> `--allow` (or SSH-level `--ssh-authorized-keys`), anyone on the
> internet who reads the TXT record can connect.

On the client machine, generate a client identity keypair. It prints
the public key, which is all the server needs to know:

```sh
client$ tailcat genkey --client --key=client-default
# wrote file to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/client-default.private.json
nodekey:cfb6bfa77a0654d7450947fd6acef17d2cd848da1d30b2540b13dac272ddfd16
```

On the server, generate a server keypair pinned to its nearest DERP
region (see why below), then serve SSH to only that client:

```sh
server$ tailcat genkey --key=default --fixed-region
# wrote file to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/default.private.json
tcXXXXXXXXX

server$ tailcat serve --allow=nodekey:cfb6bf...ddfd16 22
# 🐈 Server listening with saved key "default": tcXXXXXXXXX
```

Publish the tailcat address in DNS as a TXT record:

```
my-server.example.com. 300 IN TXT "tailcat=tcXXXXXXXXX"
```

And then the client side is just:

```sh
client$ tailcat ssh my-server.example.com
```

Client modes automatically use the saved `client-default` key when it
exists, so no extra flags are needed to present the allowed identity.
Anyone else's handshake is silently ignored: they can't reach the SSH
server, or even learn that one is running.

# NVIDIA Run:ai

[![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai)](LICENSE)
[![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/static-code-analysis.yaml?branch=main&label=CI)](.github/workflows/static-code-analysis.yaml)

[![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai)](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/graphs/contributors)

[Docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/) | [Roadmap](#roadmap) | [Installation](#installation) | [API Reference](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/reference/home) | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) | [License](#license)

**NVIDIA Run:ai is an open-source AI workload and GPU orchestration platform** for managing shared AI infrastructure on Kubernetes.

NVIDIA Run:ai provides a consistent way to run development, training, and inference workloads across Kubernetes environments, whether deployed on-premises, in the cloud, or across hybrid infrastructure. It combines GPU scheduling, resource management, workload orchestration, governance, and observability to help organizations share GPU resources efficiently across teams and clusters.

This monorepo contains the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and cluster services, installer, CLI, MCP server, documentation, shared client packages, and the local development environment.

## Architecture

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/assets/system-overview.png" alt="NVIDIA Run:ai system overview" width="900" />
</p>

**[Architecture Overview →](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/getting-started/architecture)**

NVIDIA Run:ai is made up of two components, both installed on a Kubernetes cluster:

- NVIDIA Run:ai control plane - Provides centralized resource management, handles workload submission, and delivers cluster monitoring and analytics. The control plane is the management layer; it connects to one or more NVIDIA Run:ai clusters and gives administrators and users a single place to operate across them.
- NVIDIA Run:ai cluster - Set of cluster services that provide enhanced scheduling and workload management on each Kubernetes cluster where workloads run. The cluster component extends Kubernetes native scheduling with Run:ai’s GPU-aware capabilities.

At a high level:

- Users and external systems interact with NVIDIA Run:ai through the web UI, CLI, or REST API.
- The NVIDIA Run:ai control plane manages workloads, organizational resources, policies, and configuration across connected Kubernetes clusters.
- NVIDIA Run:ai cluster services synchronize configuration and workload requests from the control plane to the appropriate cluster.
- NVIDIA Run:ai applies scheduling and resource policies to determine where and how workloads run on available GPU and compute resources.
- Workload and cluster status is synchronized back to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane, providing centralized visibility across connected clusters.

### Core Capabilities

| Capability                        | What it does                                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **AI-aware GPU scheduling**       | Schedules GPU workloads using fair-share, preemption, bin-packing, priorities, and topology-aware placement.                                |
| **Dynamic GPU allocation**        | Shares GPU resources across workloads with fractional GPU allocation and dynamic use of available capacity.                                 |
| **Resource quotas and policies**  | Allocates GPU resources across departments and projects and enforces organizational resource policies.                                      |
| **Multi-cluster management**      | Centrally manages workloads, resources, and configuration across multiple Kubernetes clusters.                                              |
| **AI workload management**        | Manages workspaces, training, distributed training, and inference, with extensible support for additional Kubernetes workloads.             |
| **Access control and governance** | Controls access to NVIDIA Run:ai resources with role-based permissions and enforces organizational policies across workloads and resources. |
| **Monitoring and observability**  | Provides visibility into clusters, nodes, GPUs, workloads, resource utilization, and platform activity.                                     |
| **Multiple interfaces**           | Supports NVIDIA Run:ai operations through the web UI, CLI, and REST API.                                                                     |

## How NVIDIA Run:ai Relates to Other Tools

NVIDIA Run:ai is a scheduling and orchestration layer on top of Kubernetes: it does not replace Kubernetes, a container runtime, or a CI/CD system.

| Layer | Tools | How NVIDIA Run:ai relates |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster orchestration | Kubernetes, OpenShift | NVIDIA Run:ai runs **on** these. It extends the cluster with GPU-aware scheduling rather than replacing native scheduling. |
| Schedulers | Default `kube-scheduler`, Volcano, Kueue | NVIDIA Run:ai ships the [KAI Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler) and adds fair-share, preemption, fractional GPUs, and quota hierarchies across departments and projects. |
| GPU enablement | NVIDIA GPU Operator, Network Operator | Complementary: these expose and configure GPUs on nodes; NVIDIA Run:ai decides which workloads get them and for how long. |
| ML platforms and pipelines | Kubeflow, Ray, Argo Workflows, Slurm | Complementary for the Kubernetes-based ones: they submit workloads, NVIDIA Run:ai schedules and governs the GPU capacity those workloads consume. Slurm is an alternative for HPC-style batch on bare metal. |
| Workload types | Training Operator, LeaderWorkerSet, Knative, KServe | NVIDIA Run:ai integrates with these to manage workspaces, training, distributed training, and inference as first-class workloads. |

If you need GPU sharing, quota enforcement, and multi-tenant governance across teams sharing one Kubernetes GPU estate, that is the gap NVIDIA Run:ai fills. If you only need to run a single team's jobs on dedicated GPUs, native Kubernetes scheduling may be sufficient.

| **MCP Server**                  | [`runai-mcp-server/`](runai-mcp-server)                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Model Context Protocol server that exposes NVIDIA Run:ai operations as tools for AI assistants                    |
| **Clients and shared packages** | [`runai-clients/`](runai-clients), [`runai-common-packages/`](runai-common-packages), [`runai-application-packages/`](runai-application-packages) | Generated API clients and shared Go libraries                                                                     |
| **Scale/Load Testing**          | [`scale-tests/`](scale-tests)                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Load-testing SDK and unified load-test suite used to validate platform behavior at scale                          |
| **Documentation**               | [`docs/`](docs/), [`fern/`](fern/)                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Product and developer documentation |
| **Local environment**           | [`local-dev.sh`](local-dev.sh), [`local-dev.md`](local-dev.md)                                                                                                                                | One-command local Kubernetes (Kind) development environment                                                       |

For a detailed breakdown of individual services and components, see the [Service Reference](docs/developer/services.md).

## Usage

### Local Development Environment

The [`local-dev.sh`](local-dev.sh) script builds the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and cluster services from source and deploys them to a self-contained [Kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) cluster with a local image registry.

```bash
./local-dev.sh                                  # full build + cluster + deploy
./local-dev.sh --skip-build --skip-cluster      # re-deploy only
./local-dev.sh --teardown                       # tear the environment down
```

See [Local Development Guide](local-dev.md) for prerequisites (Docker/Podman, `make`, `git`, `curl`, `python3`, `openssl`, and minimum CPU/RAM/disk; `kind`, `kubectl`, and `helm` are installed automatically) and all available flags. Go, Node, and Java are not needed on the host: all builds run inside containers.

### Building Individual Services

Each service directory has a Makefile with standard targets (`make build`, `make test`, `make lint`, `make validate`) and a README describing how to build, test, and work with that service. See the [Service Reference](docs/developer/services.md) for a breakdown of individual services and components.

## Installation

NVIDIA Run:ai can be deployed on Kubernetes or OpenShift in connected or air-gapped environments. To understand the full installation lifecycle, see the [Installation and Configuration Overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/installation-and-configuration/overview).

**Before you start:**

- **[Support Matrix](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/installation-and-configuration/support-matrix)** - Kubernetes/OpenShift versions, operating systems, GPU and network operators, and third-party services NVIDIA Run:ai supports.
- **[System Requirements](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/installation-and-configuration/system-requirements)** - Infrastructure, networking, and access you need to prepare before installing.

Choose an installation method based on how you want to manage the deployment:

- **[Guided installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/installation-and-configuration/install/guided-installation) (recommended)** - Uses the `runai-installer` CLI with a configuration YAML file. The installer performs preflight checks, installs required dependencies, and deploys the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and cluster.

- **[Manual installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/run-ai/self-hosted/documentation/installation-and-configuration/install/manual-helm/preparations)** - Deploys the NVIDIA Run:ai Helm charts directly. Use this path if you manage deployments through your own tooling, such as Argo CD, or require granular control over Helm values.

To build and run NVIDIA Run:ai locally for development, see [Usage](#usage).

### Distribution Channels

Released NVIDIA Run:ai container images are published to the NVIDIA NGC container registry under `nvcr.io/nvidia/runai-oss`, and the Helm charts to `https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia/runai-oss`: these are the locations the installer and Helm charts pull from by default. Source releases and their notes are on the [GitHub Releases page](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/releases); see [Release Process](RELEASE.md) for how releases are cut and versioned.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. Please read [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the development workflow, branch and PR policy, and CI expectations, and [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) for community guidelines.

## Roadmap

NVIDIA Run:ai does not publish a long-range feature roadmap in this repository. What is planned and in progress is tracked in the open:

- **[Open issues](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/issues)** - Planned work, accepted feature requests, and known gaps. Issues are triaged and labelled by maintainers.
- **[Releases](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/releases)** - What actually shipped in each version, with notes generated from the merged pull requests on that release branch.
- **[Support](SUPPORT.md)** - Which versions are currently supported and when each moves to end of life.

Release cadence, branch naming, and who cuts a release are documented in [Release Process](RELEASE.md).

**Known limitations:** the root `Makefile` targets are placeholders; real build, test, and lint targets live in each service directory (see [Building Individual Services](#building-individual-services)). The full CI gate runs remotely and is reported back on pull requests as the `Validate Successful Run` check.

## Community

- **[GitHub Issues](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai/issues)** - Bug reports, feature requests, documentation issues, and usage questions. This is the project's primary discussion forum; start here.
